title: Astrid y Gastón Opened French and Became Peruvian One Dish at a Time
dek: In 1994 Gastón Acurio and Astrid Gutsche opened a borrowed-money restaurant serving the French food their customers expected, then changed it one dish at a time.

story.event: Opening as a French haute-cuisine restaurant in Lima and gradually turning it into a Peruvian one
story.summary: Gastón Acurio and Astrid Gutsche, who met while training as cooks in Paris, opened Astrid y Gastón at Cantuarias 175 in Miraflores, Lima, on 14 July 1994 with US$45,000 lent by relatives and friends, as a French haute-cuisine restaurant. Afraid of losing customers who equated fine dining with Europe, they replaced French dishes with Peruvian ones gradually, and after about five years defined it as a restaurant of Peruvian haute cuisine.
paragraphs: In October 1993, by his own later account, Gastón Acurio arrived in Lima with Astrid Gutsche, the pastry cook he had met in Paris. Both had left conventional careers to cook. His family, he wrote, did not greet them with flowers: for years they had believed their son would become a prominent politician, and Europe was sending him back a humble cook. Astrid was pregnant, and they had no money and no work. When he cooked for his father after Paris, he told Andina in 2005, his father ate with disdain, as if the food tasted of betrayal.

Within weeks Astrid was working at a pastry shop and Gastón at a cookery institute, while they hunted for premises and backers. They found a house at Cantuarias 175 in Miraflores, persuaded relatives and friends, who had, he later said, little faith but great affection, to lend them US$45,000, and directed the renovation themselves. On the afternoon of 14 July 1994 Astrid y Gastón opened, advertised in the newspaper as "Haute Cuisine". The aim, he wrote twenty years later, was a French restaurant made by Peruvian cooks: French technique was what they had trained in and what diners with money expected.

The turn did not happen in one night. In a 2016 interview Acurio recalled the cooks asking why they were importing frozen mushrooms from France when Peru had so much of its own, "but we were afraid of losing our customers if we changed our direction." For those customers, he said, fine dining meant Europe and Peruvian food meant family meals at home. So they began by slipping a few ceviches onto a menu of foie gras terrines. Year by year, in his telling, foie gras, tartares and burgundies gave way to ceviches, tacu tacu and saltados, while they kept what Europe had taught them.

After about five years, he said in a 2006 speech, they had finally found their philosophy and defined the place as a restaurant of Peruvian haute cuisine. Their first venture abroad, in Chile, followed. By January 2014, when it left Cantuarias for an old hacienda in San Isidro, it had just been named Latin America's best restaurant; Acurio credited a whole generation of cooks who had felt the same pull.

quote.text: Have you never heard how the youth of Shou-ling went to study at Han-tan? They did not learn what they wanted at Han-tan, and forgot all they knew before into the bargain, so that they returned home in disgrace.
quote.thinker: Zhuangzi (words given to Prince Mou of Wei)
quote.source_title: Chuang Tzŭ: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, tr. Herbert A. Giles, Project Gutenberg eBook #59709
quote.connection: The young men who went to Han-tan to copy its manners came home having lost their own. Acurio and Gutsche went abroad to learn and came home to imitate; their slow turn kept what Paris taught them without forgetting what Lima already knew.

reflection: Most of us carry a borrowed picture of what serious work should look like: the way respected people elsewhere do it, the format a funder expects, the habits of the place we trained. Acurio and Gutsche did not throw theirs out in one brave night. They were afraid of losing the customers they had, so they put a few ceviches on the menu and watched.

The change took years and kept what was good in the training. Your own turn towards what is yours can be that slow. It still counts while it is happening, even on the days when you are too tired to move it any further.
invitation: Choose one thing in your work that you do a borrowed way out of habit. This week, try one small version of it your own way, a single ceviche on the menu, and notice who responds.

cross_checks.claim: Astrid y Gastón opened on 14 July 1994 at Cantuarias 175 in Miraflores
It opened as a French restaurant
The start-up money was US$45,000 lent by relatives and friends
The change to Peruvian cooking was gradual, with Peruvian dishes added to a French menu before the restaurant was redefined as Peruvian haute cuisine

research_notes: Timing of the change: Acurio's accounts differ in emphasis. His 2014 letter says the shift came little by little, year by year, almost from the first day; in the 2016 Daily Meal interview he says 'one day it all changed' and that 'after a couple of years' they had a strategy; in his 2006 Universidad del Pacífico speech he says that after five years they had found their philosophy and defined themselves as Peruvian haute cuisine. The story therefore presents a gradual change and dates the redefinition to 'about five years' on his 2006 account. The letter and speech are in Spanish; the story paraphrases them in English and uses quotation marks only for the newspaper notice ('Haute Cuisine', quoted in the letter as printed) and for Acurio's own English words in the Daily Meal interview. The father's reaction is reported by Andina's 2005 profile, partly in Acurio's words ('le sabía a traición') and partly as the journalist's gloss; the story attributes it to that interview. Funding: the slate said bootstrapped; the sources say the US$45,000 was borrowed from relatives and friends, with no outside investors mentioned, so 'bootstrapped' is kept. Astrid Gutsche's surname appears as Gutsche and Gutché; Living in Peru describes her as originally from Germany and trained in pastry, and the Daily Meal calls her a pastry chef, so the story calls her a pastry cook. The IDB page, Andina profile and Universidad del Pacífico speech are cited from Internet Archive copies because the live IDB page returns 403 and the other two are offline. The quote: Giles notes that this episode of chapter XVII, in which Prince Mou of Wei rebukes the logician Kung Sun Lung, is probably a later addition to the book; it is attributed to the book Zhuangzi and the speaker is named.
